If I was to scale a business to six figures within a year, from scratch, tomorrow, here’s exactly how I’d do it.

Week 1: Market research

I’d spend the whole week finding the gaps in the market before I tried to sell a single thing. 

This is where most people go wrong: they build something and realise that either A) No one needs it or B) No one will pay for it

Weeks 2-4: ICP interviews

I’d get on calls with as many potential customers as I could and ask them everything.

Where they look when they want to buy, how they buy, what they need to see before they say yes, and what contract terms they actually prefer.

Then I’d let them make the offer for me.

Ask enough of the right people and they’ll tell you exactly what they’d pay for and how they want it packaged.

Months 1-2: Outbound and inbound at the same time

Outbound would be very soft and heavily personalised.

I’d offer the service for free or heavily discounted to a handful of target brands, in return for a case study, testimonial and an extended contract if we hit agreed deliverables.

It’s exactly how we started. Our first client paid us £0, our second paid £150, and our third paid £5k a month.

Inbound would be content, and lots of it. LinkedIn, YouTube, short-form, anywhere the right people would start seeing me as someone who really knows the space.

By month 2 I’d want a few case studies done and a proper operating manual for delivery, written well enough that someone else could pick it up and run most of it.

This is the bit I’d change most from last time.

For the first 3 years of Augmentum we hired nobody, then we hired 20 people in 18 months. 

If I did it again, I’d have that manual written by month 2 and someone else running delivery soon after.

If you’re the only person that can deliver, you’re not a founder - you’re a freelancer.

Months 3-6: Move as fast as humanly possible

Sign brands, bring people in, push revenue as hard as it’ll go.

And use the chaos to learn two things:

→ How the offer and ICP change once real clients are paying, and which parts of the system break first so you can make them bulletproof

→ How much AI can genuinely do, which bits actually need a human, and what that means for your hiring plan

Months 6-12: Make your critical hires

Who they are depends on what you’re selling.

But by this point the business will have told you exactly where it’s breaking, and that’s where your first big hires go.

That’s the plan I’d run.

An AI knowledge base built from your own documents, without hiring AI engineers. Here's the problem it solves, explained simply.
⠀
The problem
Most of what a business knows lives in documents: price lists, policies, contracts, handbooks, meeting notes, sales decks. You pay for AI subscriptions every month, but when you ask a real question ("Can a customer get a refund on an annual plan after 30 days?"), the AI has no idea. It has never seen your files. Every new chat starts from zero, so you upload the same files again and again, and they are forgotten when the chat ends.
⠀
The slow, expensive way
You can hire AI engineers to build a knowledge base for you. That means a pipeline to read your files, "chunking" (cutting documents into small passages), "embeddings" (turning each passage into numbers that capture its meaning, so the AI can search by meaning, not just keywords) and a vector database to store and search them. It works, but it takes months and a big upfront bill before the first answer.
⠀
The way on SVAHNAR: Knowledge Repositories
1. Create a Knowledge Repository and upload your documents (PDFs, sheets, docs, slides).
2. SVAHNAR reads them, splits them and indexes them for you. No pipeline or database to run.
3. Connect your custom agents to it: a support agent, a sales agent, or your own personal assistant. Create as many repositories as you need, and connect each agent to the ones it needs.
4. Ask the same question again: the agent searches your documents and answers, showing the file and page it used, so you can check it.
⠀
Why it matters
The AI you already pay for finally works with what you know: your business knowledge, or your own notes and files, turned into real action. Upload once, and any agent you connect can use it.

Everyone's talking about who can register as a Consent Manager. 🔔

Most businesses have a smaller, more useful first job.

Quick facts:
📌 Consent Manager registration opens from Nov 2026, for Indian companies with at least ₹2 crore net worth
📌 The core DPDP duties start around 13 May 2027

So what should a business do first? A consent journey audit:

1⃣ List every customer journey that touches personal data: sign-up, KYC, marketing, support, app permissions, children's accounts.

2⃣ Name the lawful ground for each one: consent, or one of the Act's "legitimate uses". That list is narrower than GDPR's, and there is no general "contract" ground.

3⃣ For consent-based journeys, check: Is the notice clear? Is withdrawing as easy as giving consent? Do you keep a record? For under-18s, is parental consent verifiable?

4⃣ Test it like a release. Click through each journey and compare what you collect with what you recorded.

The result is a one-page map that tells a team where to focus first.

We spent years trying to make software faster. 

Now, we have a brand-new problem: understanding what we just built.

According to TestMu AI’s State of AI in Quality Engineering 2026 report, 81% of software teams admit they have merged AI-written code they did not fully understand. 

Among developers, that number jumps to 93%. 

Meanwhile, 44% of teams report more bugs escaping into production as AI takes over more of the keyboard.   

Think about what that means outside of engineering. Imagine hiring a brilliant ghostwriter who turns around a 50-page contract in ten seconds. 

It looks polished, reads smoothly, and passes a quick glance. 

So you sign it. 

Months later, you realize nobody in your company actually knows what is buried in clause fourteen.

Writing code is no longer the bottleneck in tech. 

Verifying it is. 

When teams spend half their energy generating output and a fraction of it checking the work, speed quietly turns into hidden debt.  
 
The most valuable skill in the AI era isn’t prompting faster. 

It’s having the judgment, curiosity, and discipline to slow down and verify what ships before your customers find the flaws for you.

Automate everything is bad advice. Automate the right things instead.

The 4-question test — automate only if all four are yes:
1. Is it repeated?
2. Are the steps clear?
3. Is a mistake cheap to fix?
4. Does it need no empathy?

Then sort into three tiers:
• Automate: invoice matching, data entry, scheduling, weekly reports
• Automate with a human check: support drafts, lead scoring, contract first pass
• Keep human: pricing exceptions, hiring, performance reviews, the unhappy-client call

Why it matters: 76% of small businesses use AI, only 14% have fully integrated it — and 64% of customers would prefer companies did not use AI for customer service. The line is not what AI can do. It is what a mistake costs, and who owns the decision.

Most Indian Data Engineers think "getting a job in Dubai" means automatic wealth.

Then they land here on an AED 14,000/month contract and realize they had a better life in Bangalore at ₹24 LPA.

Living and working here in the UAE as a Senior Data Engineer, here is the brutal truth nobody tells you before you apply:

There isn't ONE Dubai tech market. There are 3 completely different tiers—and picking the wrong one will set your career and savings back by 3 years.

---

TIER 3: THE "BODYSHOP" CONSULTANCIES (The Trap)
• Monthly Pay: AED 12,000 – AED 16,000
• The Reality: They hire desperate engineers from India using the "tax-free" pitch, bill the end-client AED 35,000+, and pocket the difference.
• The Perks: Zero schooling allowance, basic single medical insurance with 20% co-pays, 30% Basic Pay split (slashing your gratuity), and a 1-day probation termination clause.
• Net Savings (With Family): Zero or negative. Stay in India instead.

---

TIER 2: MID-SIZED REGIONAL ENTERPRISES & RETAIL GROUPS
• Monthly Pay: AED 20,000 – AED 26,000
• The Reality: Direct permanent payroll inside established UAE retail, logistics, or real estate groups.
• The Perks: Standard 50% Basic Pay ratio, family visa + health insurance included, annual flight tickets to India, and stable 5-day workweeks.
• Net Savings: AED 5,000 – AED 8,000/month (~₹1.15L – ₹1.85L INR).

---

TIER 1: UAE MEGA-BANKS, SOVEREIGN AI FUNDS, AIRLINES & TECH GIANTS
(Emirates NBD, FAB, ADIA, G42, Careem, Noon, Emirates Group)
• Monthly Pay: AED 28,000 – AED 45,000+
• The Reality: High-scale production ownership. You don't get hired here by listing 15 tools on a 4-page CV—you get hired by proving you can optimize terabyte-scale pipelines and cut cloud costs.
• The Perks: VIP family medical (zero co-pay), child education allowance (AED 25k–40k/year per child), 3 to 6 months annual bonus, and elite job security.
• Net Savings: AED 14,000 – AED 22,000+/month (~₹3.2L – ₹5L+ INR).

---

THE RULE FOR 2026:
Never resign from a solid product or MNC role in India to join a Tier-3 bodyshop in Dubai. 

Wait, prepare, bypass third-party agencies, and only relocate when you crack a direct Tier-2 or Tier-1 payroll offer.

We still talk about billing as a headcount problem. It is quietly becoming a skills problem. Clearinghouse edits, eligibility checks and claim scrubbing now run without a human in the loop, which means the value has moved to the exceptions nobody can automate.

Five things I would tell anyone building a career here right now:

1) Learn the data layer. Querying denial trends by payer, CARC and product line beats keying faster than the person next to you.

2) Own one payer end to end. Know its contract, fee schedule and denial profile better than the payer does. That expertise is scarce.

3) Practise the five-minute explanation. The analyst who can walk a CFO through a 4% net collection drop gets the next role.

4) Sit with coders, the front desk and contracting. Hybrid knowledge is the moat.

5) Treat AI as a teammate to supervise, not a threat to outrun.

Honest question for the group: if you were hiring tomorrow, would you teach billing to a data person, or data to a billing person?

Earlier this year I wrote about United States v. Heppner, the ruling that a defendant’s conversations with a public AI tool were not privileged. A LOT has happened since. These rules are being written right now, one case at a time, and they reach anyone who creates, builds, or runs a business with AI. Here are five cases with developments in 2026 that should shape how we work with AI going into 2027.

1. Do not assume your AI conversations are privileged.

United States v. Heppner (S.D.N.Y., February). A defendant used Claude independently to work through his case and later shared the results with his lawyers. The court held those documents were neither privileged nor protected work product. Counsel had not directed the work, and the documents did not reflect counsel’s strategy. Other courts have protected AI-assisted litigation work in different circumstances. Protection depends on the facts. Treat what you type into a consumer AI tool as something that could be read in court.

2. Your image licenses and model releases need to address AI.

Pujols v. Rainbow USA (N.Y. Sup. Ct., 2026). A model alleges Rainbow exceeded her license by using AI-altered images showing her in poses, wardrobe, and settings she never approved. Rainbow says her release allowed alterations and composites. In July, the court denied her request to halt the images while the case proceeds. The scope of her release is central to the dispute. Put in writing what AI may and may not do with someone’s likeness.

3. Know which parts of your AI-assisted work you can protect.

Thaler v. Perlmutter (cert. denied, March). The Supreme Court declined review, leaving the D.C. Circuit’s decision in place: work created entirely by AI, with no human author, cannot receive copyright protection. Human contributions to AI-assisted work can still qualify. The question is which expressive elements a human actually authored. Allen v. Perlmutter is a case to watch.

4. “AI could have made it” is not a defense to copying your work.

Vedros v. Sterling Group (M.D. Pa., May). A photographer sued a puppy seller that copied his campaign photo for a blog post. The seller argued the photo lacked market value because AI could have generated something similar. The court rejected that argument and granted summary judgment for the photographer on liability.

5. Ask hard questions about the AI tools you buy.

Mobley v. Workday (N.D. Cal., March and June). Discrimination claims involving Workday’s AI screening tools survived dismissal, based on its alleged role as the employers’ agent. Vendor liability depends on the vendor’s role and conduct. If AI touches your hiring, ask your vendor what bias testing they have done and what your contract says about it.

Whether you use AI to create, to hire, or to build your next product, this is a good moment to look at both your contracts and your habits. Which of these surprised you?

Got a "career opportunity" tonight: Director of Applied AI at… [Company/Organization]. They didn't even fill in the template.

The role is Part-Time / Contract / Board Appointment. All three, apparently. No company name, no pay, and no name under "Best regards." Just one ask, made twice: send your résumé and executive bio.

That's the whole play. They don't want to hire you, they want your details for the next con. It even passes SPF and DKIM, because it came from a throwaway Gmail. Passing email authentication only tells you who sent it, not whether they're honest.

If a recruiter can't name the company, there's no job. Delete, report, move on.

A bad offshore hire is expensive. A reversible offshore hire is manageable.

That’s the real shift most employers miss.

Offshore hiring feels risky when you assume you’re stuck if the person isn’t a fit.

The risk drops when the model is built for fast verification, not blind trust. HireNewTalent.ai is month-to-month, with free replacement and immediate backfill if someone doesn’t work out.

You don’t need to predict a perfect long-term fit on day one. You need enough signal to make a smart first decision.

That’s why recorded AI interviews matter. You can review video, audio, and a numeric scoring report before you spend time interviewing yourself.

My view: offshore hiring gets safer when replacement is cheap and fast, not when contracts are longer.

If lock-in has been the blocker, would month-to-month be enough to test one role?
